captions.text: Welcome to Module 4.
This is the module where we build our first real AI agent.
The word agent is used for almost everything these days, so before we write any
code, let's get a clear, simple definition that you can actually use.
By the end of this module, you'll have built a smart calculator agent from scratch,
and you'll understand every line of it.
In this lesson, you'll learn to tell a chatbot, a workflow, and an agent apart.
You'll be able to explain who decides the next step in each one.
And you'll learn to choose the simplest design that does the job, which is often not
an agent.
Let's start with a quick look back.
In Module 2, you learned to send a request to a language model and read its reply.
In Module 3, you got validated data back, and you split a bigger task into smaller
steps.
Now we add one new idea.
Instead of your code choosing every step, we let the model choose the next step
itself.
That one change is what turns a program into an agent.
There are three common ways to build with a language model.
The difference between them is simple: who decides what happens next?
First, a chatbot.
You send a message, and the model replies.
That's it.
If something else needs to happen, you, the human, decide what to ask next.
Second, a workflow.
Your program runs a fixed list of steps, in a fixed order, and some of those steps
are model calls.
The resume analyzer from Module 3 is a workflow: extract, compare, advise, always in
that order.
Third, an agent.
The model chooses an action, like using a tool, sees the result, and then chooses
again.
It repeats this in a loop until the job is done.
The model decides the steps, not your code.
Here's the picture we'll keep coming back to in this module.
Take your time with it.
It starts with a goal, here, a maths question.
The model reads it and decides what to do first.
Say it decides to use the calculator.
Important: the model can't run the calculator itself.
It can only ask.
Your program does the actual work.
That's the act step.
The result goes back to the model.
That's the observe step.
Now the model knows something new, so it decides again.
Maybe it needs another calculation.
And when the model decides nothing is left to do, it answers, and the loop ends.
Decide, act, observe, repeat.
That loop is the heart of every agent in this course.
So when should you use which?
Ask yourself one question: do I know the steps in advance?
If you do, use a workflow.
It's predictable, its cost is predictable, and you can test each step on its own.
If the steps depend on what you discover along the way, use an agent.
An agent is flexible, but you pay for that: its cost and time vary from run to run,
and it's harder to test.
A very practical rule: always start with the simplest design.
If one request gives you the answer, use a single call.
If the steps are fixed, use a workflow.
Reach for an agent only when the path really is unknown.
And whatever you choose, actions that are expensive or can't be undone, like paying,
deleting, or sending, need checks and limits.
We'll build those habits from this module on.
Time to check your understanding.
Pause the video, and for each of these three tasks, decide: single call, workflow,
or agent?
One.
Translate a paragraph into Spanish.
Two.
Turn a resume and a job posting into a skills-gap report.
Three.
Plan a trip within a budget, checking prices as you go.
Here are my answers.
Translation is a single call: one request, one answer.
The gap report is a workflow: the steps are always the same.
And trip planning is an agent: what to check next depends on the prices you find.
Quick check.
What makes a program an agent?
The model decides the next step, in a loop, using tools.
In a workflow, your code makes those decisions instead.
A chatbot answers one question at a time.
In a workflow, your code decides the steps.
In an agent, the model decides, acts, observes, and repeats.
And you should always choose the simplest design that works.
Next lesson, we open an agent up and look at its four parts: the model, the
instructions, the tools, and the state.
